claim: RNA interference is an ancient mechanism with many regulatory roles in eukaryotic genomes.
source: RNA interference is an ancient mechanism with many regulatory roles in eukaryotic genomes, with small RNAs acting as their functional element.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about RNAi in eukaryotes.

claim: Small RNAs act as the functional element of RNA interference.
source: RNA interference is an ancient mechanism with many regulatory roles in eukaryotic genomes, with small RNAs acting as their functional element.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of small RNAs in RNAi.

claim: MicroRNAs have distinct roles in plants and animals.
source: Such is the case of microRNAs (miRNAs), which have distinct roles in plants and animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA function across kingdoms.

claim: Fungi produce small RNAs.
source: Fungi also produce small RNAs, and several publications have identified miRNAs and miRNA-like (mi/milRNA) hairpin RNAs in diverse fungal species using deep sequencing technologies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple publications in the literature.

claim: Several publications have identified miRNAs and miRNA-like hairpin RNAs in diverse fungal species using deep sequencing technologies.
source: Fungi also produce small RNAs, and several publications have identified miRNAs and miRNA-like (mi/milRNA) hairpin RNAs in diverse fungal species using deep sequencing technologies.
evidence: This is supported by the literature review conducted in this study.

claim: Relatively little is known about mi/milRNA features in fungi.
source: Despite this relevant source of information, relatively little is known about mi/milRNA features in fungi, mostly due to a lack of established criteria for their annotation.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the state of the field as reviewed by the authors.

claim: The lack of knowledge about mi/milRNA features in fungi is mostly due to a lack of established criteria for their annotation.
source: Despite this relevant source of information, relatively little is known about mi/milRNA features in fungi, mostly due to a lack of established criteria for their annotation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' analysis of the literature.

claim: The study re-assessed annotations for 41 fungal species.
source: To systematically assess mi/milRNA characteristics and annotation confidence, we searched for publications describing mi/milRNA loci and re-assessed the annotations for 41 fungal species.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's methodology and scope.

claim: The study extracted and normalized annotation data for 1727 reported mi/milRNA loci.
source: We extracted and normalized the annotation data for 1727 reported mi/milRNA loci and determined their abundance profiles, concluding that less than half of the reported loci passed basic standards used for hairpin RNA discovery.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analyzed in the study.

claim: Less than half of the reported mi/milRNA loci passed basic standards used for hairpin RNA discovery.
source: We extracted and normalized the annotation data for 1727 reported mi/milRNA loci and determined their abundance profiles, concluding that less than half of the reported loci passed basic standards used for hairpin RNA discovery.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the re-analysis of sequencing data performed in the study.

claim: Fungal mi/milRNA are generally more similar in size to animal miRNAs.
source: We found that fungal mi/milRNA are generally more similar in size to animal miRNAs and were frequently associated with protein-coding genes.
evidence: This finding is based on the analysis of locus characteristics presented in the study.

claim: Fungal mi/milRNA were frequently associated with protein-coding genes.
source: We found that fungal mi/milRNA are generally more similar in size to animal miRNAs and were frequently associated with protein-coding genes.
evidence: This finding is based on genomic context analysis performed in the study.

claim: The compiled genomic analyses identified 25 mi/milRNA loci conserved in multiple species.
source: The compiled genomic analyses identified 25 mi/milRNA loci conserved in multiple species.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the conservation analysis results.

claim: The study identified more than 150 loci with high-quality annotations.
source: Our pipeline allowed us to build a general hierarchy of locus quality, identifying more than 150 loci with high-quality annotations.
evidence: This is based on the tier classification system developed in the study.

claim: Small regulatory RNAs are typically 20–24 nucleotides in length.
source: Small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are the functional elements behind RNAi and are typically 20–24 nucleotides in length.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sRNA characteristics.

claim: Small RNAs play key roles in genome stability.
source: Functionally, sRNAs play key roles in genome stability (Lewsey et al., 2016; Nolan et al., 2005), protection against RNA-based organisms (Nicolás and Ruiz-Vázquez, 2013; Segers et al., 2007), and regulation of gene expression (Jones-Rhoades et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Small RNAs play key roles in protection against RNA-based organisms.
source: Functionally, sRNAs play key roles in genome stability (Lewsey et al., 2016; Nolan et al., 2005), protection against RNA-based organisms (Nicolás and Ruiz-Vázquez, 2013; Segers et al., 2007), and regulation of gene expression (Jones-Rhoades et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Small RNAs play key roles in regulation of gene expression.
source: Functionally, sRNAs play key roles in genome stability (Lewsey et al., 2016; Nolan et al., 2005), protection against RNA-based organisms (Nicolás and Ruiz-Vázquez, 2013; Segers et al., 2007), and regulation of gene expression (Jones-Rhoades et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Fungal sRNAs have been shown to display trans-kingdom functions.
source: In the context of pathogenic organisms, such as fungal plant pathogens, sRNAs have even been shown to display trans-kingdom functions (Wang et al., 2017a; Weiberg et al., 2013), where fungal sRNAs serve as effectors of pathogenicity regulating host genes to undermine resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Fungal sRNAs serve as effectors of pathogenicity regulating host genes to undermine resistance.
source: In the context of pathogenic organisms, such as fungal plant pathogens, sRNAs have even been shown to display trans-kingdom functions (Wang et al., 2017a; Weiberg et al., 2013), where fungal sRNAs serve as effectors of pathogenicity regulating host genes to undermine resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Regions of double-stranded RNA are processed by a Type-III RNAse called Dicer or Dicer-like.
source: Regions of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) are processed by a Type-III RNAse called Dicer or Dicer-like (collectively abbreviated here as DCR), producing sRNA duplexes which are subsequently loaded in an Argonaute protein (AGO) for their resulting function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RNAi pathway.

claim: Dicer processing produces sRNA duplexes which are subsequently loaded in an Argonaute protein for their resulting function.
source: Regions of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) are processed by a Type-III RNAse called Dicer or Dicer-like (collectively abbreviated here as DCR), producing sRNA duplexes which are subsequently loaded in an Argonaute protein (AGO) for their resulting function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RNAi pathway.

claim: DCRs are responsible for the resulting sRNA length.
source: DCRs are responsible for the resulting sRNA length (Macrae et al., 2006) and these lengths are selective for the specific AGO loading.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: sRNA lengths are selective for specific AGO loading.
source: DCRs are responsible for the resulting sRNA length (Macrae et al., 2006) and these lengths are selective for the specific AGO loading.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sRNA-AGO interactions.

claim: DCRs directly influence sRNA function.
source: As a result, DCRs directly influence sRNA function (Fang and Qi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Two main pathways exist for dsRNA production: dsRNA produced through synthesis by an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and complementary regions in transcripts forming stem-loop foldback structures known as hairpins.
source: Two main pathways exist for this: (1) dsRNA produced through synthesis by an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDR) and (2) complementary regions in transcripts form stem-loop foldback structures known as hairpins (Axtell, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Hairpin-derived sRNAs are widespread in eukaryotes.
source: Hairpin-derived sRNAs (hpRNAs) are widespread in eukaryotes and include microRNAs (miRNAs), which have central roles in gene expression control in plants and animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hpRNAs in eukaryotes.

claim: MicroRNAs have central roles in gene expression control in plants and animals.
source: Hairpin-derived sRNAs (hpRNAs) are widespread in eukaryotes and include microRNAs (miRNAs), which have central roles in gene expression control in plants and animals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA function.

claim: Highly precise dicing characterizes miRNAs.
source: Highly precise dicing characterizes miRNAs, with the most-abundant sequences (MASs) coming from a single duplex in the 5' and 3' hairpin arms (Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The most-abundant sequences of miRNAs come from a single duplex in the 5' and 3' hairpin arms.
source: Highly precise dicing characterizes miRNAs, with the most-abundant sequences (MASs) coming from a single duplex in the 5' and 3' hairpin arms (Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In plants, miRNAs function mostly through direct cleavage of a target mRNA.
source: In plants, miRNAs function mostly through direct cleavage of a target mRNA (Rogers and Chen, 2013), whereas in animals the process is less straightforward, relying on inhibition of translation and mRNA de-tailing, de-capping, and degradation by exonucleases (Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In animals, miRNA function relies on inhibition of translation and mRNA de-tailing, de-capping, and degradation by exonucleases.
source: In plants, miRNAs function mostly through direct cleavage of a target mRNA (Rogers and Chen, 2013), whereas in animals the process is less straightforward, relying on inhibition of translation and mRNA de-tailing, de-capping, and degradation by exonucleases (Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A significant number of miRNA are anciently conserved in sequence and function.
source: A significant number of miRNA are anciently conserved in sequence and function (Cuperus et al., 2011), though they may also be highly clade- or species-specific (Fahlgren et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: miRNAs may be highly clade- or species-specific.
source: A significant number of miRNA are anciently conserved in sequence and function (Cuperus et al., 2011), though they may also be highly clade- or species-specific (Fahlgren et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Most miRNAs come from intergenic or untranslated genic regions (introns, UTRs).
source: Most miRNAs come from intergenic or untranslated genic regions (introns, UTRs), and there are rare if any examples of miRNAs derived from coding sequences (CDS) (Liu et al., 2018; Olena and Patton, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: There are rare if any examples of miRNAs derived from coding sequences.
source: Most miRNAs come from intergenic or untranslated genic regions (introns, UTRs), and there are rare if any examples of miRNAs derived from coding sequences (CDS) (Liu et al., 2018; Olena and Patton, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The hpRNA class of miRNA-like RNAs (milRNAs) was first identified in Neurospora crassa.
source: The hpRNA class of miRNA-like RNAs (milRNAs) was first identified in Neurospora crassa (Necra), where they follow the same schema: RNA foldbacks are processed by one of two redundant DCRs (NcDCL1 and NcDCL2), which are subsequently loaded into an AGO protein (QDE2) (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In Neurospora crassa, RNA foldbacks are processed by one of two redundant DCRs (NcDCL1 and NcDCL2), which are subsequently loaded into an AGO protein (QDE2).
source: The hpRNA class of miRNA-like RNAs (milRNAs) was first identified in Neurospora crassa (Necra), where they follow the same schema: RNA foldbacks are processed by one of two redundant DCRs (NcDCL1 and NcDCL2), which are subsequently loaded into an AGO protein (QDE2) (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Homolog proteins of the DCR and AGO families have been identified in many fungal species.
source: Homolog proteins of the DCR and AGO families have been identified in many fungal species (Choi et al., 2014) and are involved in milRNA biogenesis and function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: DCR and AGO homolog proteins are involved in milRNA biogenesis and function.
source: Homolog proteins of the DCR and AGO families have been identified in many fungal species (Choi et al., 2014) and are involved in milRNA biogenesis and function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Over 60 publications have cited hpRNAs in fungi, using the designations miRNA or milRNA.
source: Since, over 60 publications have cited hpRNAs in fungi, using the designations miRNA or milRNA (collectively referred to as mi/milRNAs).
evidence: This is based on the literature search conducted in the study.

claim: In fungi, mi/milRNAs have been identified frequently in the context of pathogenesis.
source: In fungi, these sRNAs have been identified frequently in the context of pathogenesis (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Some fungal mi/milRNAs are proposed to regulate gene expression in trans, regulating plant and animal host gene expression.
source: This also includes some proposed to regulate gene expression in trans (Cui et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017b; Wong-Bajracharya et al., 2022), regulating plant and animal host gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Most fungal mi/milRNA studies lack clear evidence for the causative role of the sRNA in the process.
source: However, most lack clear evidence for the causative role of the sRNA in the process, as many studies rely on target prediction alone for understanding their biological role (Pinzón et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an assessment based on the literature review and supported by a citation.

claim: The advent of small-RNA-seq technology has massively increased the amount of data available for detecting sRNA-producing loci.
source: The advent of small-RNA-seq technology has massively increased the amount of data available for detecting sRNA-producing loci.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the impact of sequencing technology.

claim: A wide spectrum of tools are available for annotation of miRNAs.
source: A wide spectrum of tools are available for annotation of miRNAs, with most of them based on strict rules derived from characteristics that are specific to known miRNAs from plants or animals (Axtell and Meyers, 2018; Friedländer et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2016; Kuang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Most miRNA annotation tools are based on strict rules derived from characteristics specific to known miRNAs from plants or animals.
source: A wide spectrum of tools are available for annotation of miRNAs, with most of them based on strict rules derived from characteristics that are specific to known miRNAs from plants or animals (Axtell and Meyers, 2018; Friedländer et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2016; Kuang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: There has yet to be a systematic assessment of fungal mi/milRNA characteristics and annotation confidence.
source: Despite many publications identifying mi/milRNA loci in fungi, there has yet to be a systematic assessment of their characteristics and annotation confidence, as in other eukaryotic species (Kozomara and Griffiths-Jones, 2014; Meng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on the literature review.

claim: The search for publications yielded a list of 60 publications which assess fungal mi/milRNAs.
source: The search yielded a list of 60 publications which assess fungal mi/milRNAs, 53 of which performed and reported de novo mi/milRNA loci identification from sRNA-seq data (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1), using a broad range of bioinformatic tools or pipelines (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the literature search results.

claim: 53 publications performed and reported de novo mi/milRNA loci identification from sRNA-seq data.
source: The search yielded a list of 60 publications which assess fungal mi/milRNAs, 53 of which performed and reported de novo mi/milRNA loci identification from sRNA-seq data (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1), using a broad range of bioinformatic tools or pipelines (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the literature search results.

claim: The majority of sRNA-seq libraries used in fungal mi/milRNA studies are publicly available.
source: The majority of these sRNA-seq libraries are publicly available (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1) and span 41 fungal species, including some subspecies (Figure 1C), presenting a prime opportunity to uncover common fungal mi/milRNA characteristics.
evidence: This is based on the assessment of publications shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sRNA-seq libraries span 41 fungal species, including some subspecies.
source: The majority of these sRNA-seq libraries are publicly available (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1) and span 41 fungal species, including some subspecies (Figure 1C), presenting a prime opportunity to uncover common fungal mi/milRNA characteristics.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the scope of the study.

claim: Nearly all explored species are Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes.
source: Nearly all explored species are Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes, though more distant divisions of Glomeromycota and Microsporidia are also included (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: More distant divisions of Glomeromycota and Microsporidia are also included in the study.
source: Nearly all explored species are Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes, though more distant divisions of Glomeromycota and Microsporidia are also included (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only around half of the publications provide coordinates or complete sequences for precursor genes.
source: For instance, only around half of the publications provide coordinates or complete sequences for precursor genes (Figure 1B), key information to derive structural and compositional features of the hairpins and genomic contexts.
evidence: This is based on the assessment of publications shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Less than half of the published mi/milRNA have support from at least two independent biological replicates.
source: Furthermore, less than half of the published mi/milRNA have support from at least two independent biological replicates (Figure 1B), a requirement considered as vital for miRNA annotation (Axtell and Meyers, 2018).
evidence: This is based on the assessment of publications shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Support from at least two independent biological replicates is considered vital for miRNA annotation.
source: Furthermore, less than half of the published mi/milRNA have support from at least two independent biological replicates (Figure 1B), a requirement considered as vital for miRNA annotation (Axtell and Meyers, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published guidelines.

claim: A minority of the source publications for a locus provide genetic evidence to support mi/milRNA biogenesis machinery using knock-out or over-expressor lines.
source: Regarding experimental validation, a minority of the source publications for a locus provide genetic evidence to support mi/milRNA biogenesis machinery using knock-out or over-expressor lines, or explore targeting relationships with direct experimental evidence (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on the assessment of publications shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Around one-third of loci had neither an annotation associated with the full precursor sequence nor complete genomic coordinates.
source: Around one-third of loci had neither an annotation associated with the full precursor sequence nor complete genomic coordinates (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on the assessment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The hairpin precursor recovery pipeline has reasonably high accuracy for predicting the correct genomic locality.
source: This hairpin precursor recovery pipeline was evaluated in terms of precision and sensitivity for identifying the correct locality for an mi/milRNA locus as well as its folding pattern, confirming that our pipeline has reasonably high accuracy for predicting the correct genomic locality, based on the number of alignments for a cited MAS for an mi/milRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on the evaluation of the recovery pipeline shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The pipeline has solid metrics for recapitulating the same hairpin when testing against known hairpins.
source: We also found solid metrics for recapitulating the same hairpin when testing the pipeline against known hairpins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on the evaluation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Most hairpins met the minimum requirements for valid hairpins.
source: Hairpins reported in publications and obtained from the recovery pipeline were evaluated according to these standards, finding that most of them met these minimum requirements (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the assessment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Around 20% of the published loci failed one or more of the minimum hairpin tests and were excluded from further analyses.
source: Notably, around 20% of the published loci failed one or more of these tests and were excluded from further analyses (further referred to as 'invalid').
evidence: This is based on the hairpin validation analysis.

claim: Within a large proportion of loci, the mature sequence reported is not the MAS for the locus.
source: However, within a large proportion of loci, we found that the mature sequence reported is not the MAS for the locus (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on the re-analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Numerous examples of loci had no reads aligning with the reported mature sequence or loci with no reads aligned at all.
source: Even more problematic, we found numerous examples of loci that had no reads aligning with the reported mature sequence or loci with no reads aligned at all (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on the re-analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fungal sRNAs frequently fail to meet key points of plant and animal miRNA criteria.
source: Applying these criteria (summarized in Supplementary file 6), we found that fungal sRNAs frequently fail to meet key points compared to animal or plant miRNAs, resulting in very few that pass all rules in a set.
evidence: This is based on the application of established miRNA criteria to fungal loci.

claim: Fungal mi/milRNA partial fulfillment of criteria is similar to the performance of miRNAs annotated as low confidence in miRbase for plants and animals.
source: This partial fulfillment of criteria is similar to the performance of miRNAs annotated as low confidence in miRbase for plants and animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nearly half of the loci pass the three basic criteria in at least one library.
source: We found that nearly half of the loci pass these three criteria in at least one library (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Low-confidence miRNAs performed poorly in terms of strandedness and expression.
source: We found low-confidence miRNAs performed poorly, especially in terms of strandedness and expression, while for high-confidence loci more than 80% passed all three rules (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of control miRNAs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For high-confidence loci more than 80% passed all three rules.
source: We found low-confidence miRNAs performed poorly, especially in terms of strandedness and expression, while for high-confidence loci more than 80% passed all three rules (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of control miRNAs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fungal loci perform considerably worse than high-confidence Arabidopsis thaliana and Drosophila melanogaster loci in terms of passing both expression and stranding filters.
source: We found that fungal loci perform considerably worse than high-confidence Artha and Drmel loci in terms of passing both expression and stranding filters (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on the comparison shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fungal loci perform much better than low-confidence miRNA considering expression and stranding metrics.
source: However, it is noteworthy that these fungal loci still perform much better than low-confidence miRNA considering these metrics (Figure 2C), indicating that they may represent a heterogeneous mixture of sRNA, possibly including siRNA or degradation-related loci, for example.
evidence: This is based on the comparison shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 394 loci (22.8%) passed all criteria ('confirmed' set).
source: From our initial set of 1727 loci, 394 (22.8%) passed all criteria ('confirmed' set, Figure 2D, Supplementary file 4), while 272 (15.7%) passed all criteria in two or more different libraries ('confirmed and replicated' set, Figure 2D, Supplementary file 4), for a total of 666 confirmed loci.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the confirmation analysis results.

claim: 272 loci (15.7%) passed all criteria in two or more different libraries ('confirmed and replicated' set).
source: From our initial set of 1727 loci, 394 (22.8%) passed all criteria ('confirmed' set, Figure 2D, Supplementary file 4), while 272 (15.7%) passed all criteria in two or more different libraries ('confirmed and replicated' set, Figure 2D, Supplementary file 4), for a total of 666 confirmed loci.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the confirmation analysis results.

claim: 15 loci (0.9%) met the criteria and also the more strict set of rules used for plant miRNAs.
source: Interestingly, 15 (0.9%) of these loci met our criteria and also the more strict set of rules used for plant miRNAs (ShortStack and Axtell-2018) (Axtell, 2013b; Axtell and Meyers, 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: Most hairpins did not find hits in Rfam.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, most hairpins did not find hits in Rfam.
evidence: This is based on the Rfam search results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: bba-milR4 in Beauveria bassiana matches the nearly universal U6 snRNA.
source: This appears to explain some of the most repetitive sequences such as bba-milR4 in Beauveria bassiana (Bebas), which matches the nearly universal U6 snRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the Rfam search results shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: bba-milR4 matches hundreds of loci in animals and plants.
source: In this case, we find that bba-milR4 matches hundreds of loci in animals and plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and is found in the majority of other searched genomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of the confirmed/no-sequencing-evidence loci arise from coding regions within PCGs.
source: We found across species that many of the confirmed/no-sequencing-evidence loci arise from coding regions within PCGs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Very rarely, mi/milRNAs from fungi were located entirely within an intron of PCGs.
source: Very rarely, mi/milRNAs from fungi were located entirely within an intron of PCGs as one might expect from a mirtron as seen in animals (Ruby et al., 2007; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster high-confidence miRNAs, virtually all of those intersecting PCGs were found within introns.
source: In the case of Drmel high-confidence miRNAs, virtually all of those intersecting PCGs were found within introns, compared to fungi with only Cryptococcus neoformans (Crneo) showing similarly high rates of intronic mi/milRNAs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cryptococcus neoformans shows similarly high rates of intronic mi/milRNAs compared to Drosophila melanogaster.
source: In the case of Drmel high-confidence miRNAs, virtually all of those intersecting PCGs were found within introns, compared to fungi with only Cryptococcus neoformans (Crneo) showing similarly high rates of intronic mi/milRNAs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A much lower proportion of confirmed loci intersect with TEs.
source: Comparing the feature intersections of loci in regard to their confirmation status, we find that a much lower proportion of confirmed loci intersect with TEs (Figure 3D), likely a sign of incorrect annotation.
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 401 mi/milRNA loci did not intersect other genomic features (TE, PCG) and also failed to find a homolog in the Rfam dataset.
source: We found 401 mi/milRNA loci that did not intersect other genomic features (TE, PCG) and also failed to find a homolog in the Rfam dataset (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A simple search for the MAS from an mi/milRNA between sequencing libraries from different species did not reveal any conserved sequences.
source: A simple search for the MAS from an mi/milRNA between sequencing libraries from different species did not reveal any conserved sequences, leading us to explore whether hairpin sequences might be conserved.
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis performed in the study.

claim: Homologs are primarily found only in closely related species based on the strict cutoffs used.
source: Homologs are primarily found only in closely related species based on the strict cutoffs mentioned, with only three examples of homology between class-level designations (Scscl mi/milRNAs to Alternaria brassicicola – Albra, and Bodot).
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis results.

claim: Only three examples of homology between class-level designations were found.
source: Homologs are primarily found only in closely related species based on the strict cutoffs mentioned, with only three examples of homology between class-level designations (Scscl mi/milRNAs to Alternaria brassicicola – Albra, and Bodot).
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis results.

claim: milR22 from Cordyceps militaris is the most highly conserved sequence, found in 15 Sordariomycetes.
source: The most highly conserved sequence is milR22 (PID1154) from Cordyceps militaris (Comil), which is found in 15 Sordariomycetes in our assembly set (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression profiling in Cordyceps militaris shows that reads primarily come from one hairpin arm.
source: Expression profiling in Comil shows that reads primarily come from one hairpin arm, consistent with an hpRNA locus.
evidence: This is based on the expression profiling analysis.

claim: Trichoderma reesei was found to produce sRNAs from the milR22 putative hairpin with a similar profile to Cordyceps militaris.
source: Trree was found to produce sRNAs from this putative hairpin with a similar profile to Comil (Figure 4B), supporting that these may be orthologous genes.
evidence: This is based on the expression profiling shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Conservation in fungal mi/milRNAs does not compare with the magnitude in plants.
source: While there is conservation in fungal mi/milRNAs, it does not compare with the magnitude in plants, where miRNA conservation is widespread among our examined species (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Animal miRNAs show signs of conservation, though distinctly lower than plants.
source: Animal miRNAs also show signs of conservation, though distinctly lower than plants, possibly a result of their shorter hairpin lengths (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 155 loci met the distinction of falling into tiers 1 and 2.
source: Loci falling into tiers 1 and 2 were considered to have strong support as mi/milRNA loci and were compared to miRNAs in other organisms; 155 loci met this distinction, coming from 16 different fungi from diverse clades (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on the tier classification analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Rhizoctonia solani was the most commonly identified species in tiers 1 and 2.
source: The most commonly identified species was Rhizoctonia solani (Rhsol), which had the highest quantity of confirmed and replicated loci of all species (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on the tier classification analysis shown in Figure 5B and confirmation analysis in Figure 2E.

claim: Top-tier loci tend to fall into similar size ranges as sRNAs found in plants and animals.
source: These top-tier loci tend to fall into similar size ranges as sRNAs found in plants and animals (Figure 5C), though these sizes are usually more concise for miRNAs (20–22 nucleotides).
evidence: This is based on the size analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Hairpin lengths tend to be short in fungal loci, much more similar to those of animals than plants.
source: Hairpin lengths tend to be short in fungal loci, much more similar to those of animals than plants (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on the hairpin length analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The inter-duplex length for loci is usually minimally sized, and less than 20 nucleotides in all.
source: Indeed, the inter-duplex length for loci is usually minimally sized, and less than 20 nucleotides in all.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis of hairpins.

claim: MAS of top-tier mi/milRNAs in fungi comprises a much lower proportion of locus reads.
source: Here, we show that MAS of top-tier mi/milRNAs in fungi comprises a much lower proportion of locus reads (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on the dicing specificity analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Only a fraction of published fungal mi/milRNA loci remain when performing independent validation.
source: Our work finds that only a fraction of these loci remain when performing independent validation.
evidence: This is a summary of the re-analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Many loci fail minimal standards using their own sequencing data.
source: Particularly concerning are those loci failing minimal standards using their own sequencing data, pointing to a serious problem with the standards for locus identification based on sRNA-seq alignment profiles.
evidence: This is based on the re-analysis of sequencing data.

claim: Many fungal mi/milRNAs have qualities similar to low-confidence miRNAs.
source: Indeed, evidence in this work points to many fungal mi/milRNAs that have qualities similar to low-confidence miRNAs (Figure 2C), further emphasizing a need for stricter standards for annotating these loci.
evidence: This is based on the comparison with control miRNAs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only a small number of loci passed all of the rules laid out for miRNAs by some of the more strict rule sets.
source: We found that only a small number of loci passed all of the rules laid out for miRNAs by some of the more strict rule sets (Figure 3D; Axtell, 2013b; Axtell and Meyers, 2018).
evidence: This is based on the rule-based analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Confirmed hairpins in fungi are much more similar to animals in length.
source: Confirmed hairpins in fungi are much more similar to animals in length – they are very short with little to no terminal loop structure.
evidence: This is based on the hairpin length analysis.

claim: Phylogenetic comparisons of dicer proteins in eukaryotes show fungal proteins differing vastly from plants and animals.
source: Phylogenetic comparisons of dicer proteins in eukaryotes show fungal proteins differing vastly from plants and animals, where they are much more similar (Bollmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Animals have a two-step mechanism for dicing hairpins, utilizing two different RNAse III proteins (DCR and Drosha).
source: Animals have a two-step mechanism for dicing hairpins, utilizing two different RNAse III proteins (DCR and Drosha) (Axtell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: No evidence points to compartmentalization of dicing roles in fungi.
source: However, no evidence points to such a compartmentalization of dicing roles in fungi, further confounding the observed hairpin similarities.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the literature review.

claim: Fungi have an average of only two DCR homologs in a species.
source: Specific DCRs are the causative factor for determining sRNA length (Macrae et al., 2006), but fungi have an average of only two DCR homologs in a species (Choi et al., 2014) and are thought to be partially redundant in some cases (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Fungal DCR homologs are thought to be partially redundant in some cases.
source: Specific DCRs are the causative factor for determining sRNA length (Macrae et al., 2006), but fungi have an average of only two DCR homologs in a species (Choi et al., 2014) and are thought to be partially redundant in some cases (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The results point to low specificity in fungal mi/milRNA dicing.
source: Our results point to low specificity in fungal mi/milRNA dicing, which might explain the wide range of sizes observed, though this may also be a sign of clade-specific neofunctionalization of DCRs or other unknown protein factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dicing specificity analysis.

claim: There is a higher average count of AGO genes across important fungal clades.
source: As for the function of fungal sRNAs, there appears to be a higher average count of AGO genes across important clades (Choi et al., 2014), which might point to multiple roles in terms of transcriptional or post-transcriptional gene silencing.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Targeting for mi/milRNAs in Neurospora crassa appears to tolerate some degree of mismatching.
source: Targeting for mi/milRNAs in Necra appears to tolerate some degree of mismatching (Lee et al., 2010), though it is unclear what if any patterning requirements exist (i.e. seed pairing).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Three mi/milRNAs from tiers 1/2 had strong confirmed targeting.
source: Three mi/milRNAs from tiers 1/2 had strong confirmed targeting (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on the assessment of targeting evidence in the study.

claim: cci-milR-24 from Coprinopsis cinerea was shown to regulate genes involved in developmental transition.
source: One was shown in Coprinopsis cinerea (cci-milR-24, PID1279) regulating genes involved in developmental transition (Lau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Fol-milR1 and milR-87 from Fusarium oxysporum are likely paralogous loci producing the same MAS.
source: The others were identified in two different strains of Fusarium oxysporum (Fuoxy) which infect tomato (Fol-milR1, PID2279) (Ji et al., 2021) and banana (milR-87, PID2109) (Li et al., 2022), and are likely paralogous loci producing the same MAS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence similarity and supported by citations.

claim: Fol-milR1 and milR-87 targets point to both trans-species and endogenous roles in regulation.
source: Interestingly, their confirmed targets point to both trans-species and endogenous roles in regulation, targeting a tomato resistance gene (SlyFRG4) and a Fuoxy glycosyl hydrolase (FOIG_15013) linked to pathogenicity, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the targeting evidence from cited publications.

claim: Nearly all of top-tier loci are highly lineage-specific based on conservation analysis.
source: Many fungal mi/milRNAs presented here have these similar characteristics, with nearly all of top-tier loci shown as highly lineage-specific, based on our conservation analysis.
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis results.

claim: The vast majority of species analyzed are pathogens.
source: Considering that the vast majority of species analyzed here are pathogens, this could be related to adaptation to hosts and/or a function as trans-species sRNAs (Weiberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the species included in the study and supported by a citation.

claim: The most conserved locus from the work (milR22, Cordyceps militaris) is from an insect pathogen.
source: The most conserved locus from our work (milR22, Comil) is an insect pathogen (Shao et al., 2019), suggesting at a possible trans-species role.
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Many mi/milRNA loci were shown to be derived from coding sequences of genes.
source: Many mi/milRNA loci were shown to be derived from coding sequences of genes.
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis.

claim: Some work has concluded that miRNAs may be derived from rRNAs.
source: However, RDR-derived sRNAs are more frequently associated with rRNAs (Lambert et al., 2019), including the qiRNA class in fungi (Lee et al., 2009). Some evidence even points to milRNAs in Necra which might span portions of tRNAs (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: RDR-derived sRNAs are more frequently associated with rRNAs.
source: However, RDR-derived sRNAs are more frequently associated with rRNAs (Lambert et al., 2019), including the qiRNA class in fungi (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Some evidence points to milRNAs in Neurospora crassa which might span portions of tRNAs.
source: Some evidence even points to milRNAs in Necra which might span portions of tRNAs (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Around 10% of loci were found to fall in the highest tiers of support.
source: Around 10% of loci were found to fall in the highest tiers of support, with these validations and annotations provided as a community resource.
evidence: This is based on the tier classification analysis.

claim: Fungal mi/milRNAs are similar in many ways to those of animals and plants.
source: Overall, we see that fungal mi/milRNAs are similar in many ways to those of animals and plants though it is not always clear to which they are more, varying in aspects of sRNA length, hairpin length, and mode of action.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative analysis results.
